summary: הָדָר is splendour that can be seen and is worn like a garment: Yahweh is “clothed with הוֹד וְהָדָר” (Psa 104:1), he lays them on the king he saves (Psa 21:6), and it is the beauty of trees, of Carmel and Sharon, of a city, of a strong woman and of an old man’s grey hair (Lev 23:40; Isa 35:2; Pro 31:25; 20:29). The verb is to give such honour to a person, to defer to a face: to rise before the grey head and honour the old (Lev 19:32), but in judgement not to favour the great or the poor (Lev 19:15; Exo 23:3). Daniel’s Aramaic has the same verb for glorifying the King of heaven and the noun for the majesty the Most High gave Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 4:34; 5:18), and Jewish Aramaic uses both in the same senses.

words.summary: Splendour that is seen and worn: chiefly Yahweh’s own, and that which he gives to the king, to man and to his people; also the splendour of trees, land, city and people, which can be taken away or go down to the grave. It is paired with הוֹד eight times, and set beside כָּבוֹד, עֹז and תִּפְאֶרֶת.

senses.definition: The visible splendour of Yahweh as king and maker: he wears it, it is before him in his sanctuary, his work is it, and men flee from it when he rises to judge.

evidence.note: “Yahweh my God, you are very great; you are clothed with הוֹד וְהָדָר”, and in verse 2 with light as with a garment.
“הוֹד־וְהָדָר are before him, strength and beauty (תִפְאֶרֶת) in his sanctuary.”
The same words when the ark is brought up: “strength and gladness in his place”.
“His work is הוֹד־וְהָדָר, and his righteousness stands for ever.”
“The voice of Yahweh is in power; the voice of Yahweh is בֶּהָדָר.”
“The splendour of the glory of your הוֹד”: three words of glory heaped together.
To make known to the sons of man his mighty acts “and the glory of the הֲדַר of his kingdom”: the splendour is a king’s.
“Let your work appear to your servants, and your הָדָר to their children.”
“Go into the rock and hide in the dust from the terror of Yahweh and from the הֲדַר of his majesty (גְּאֹנוֹ).”
“… when he arises to shake the earth.”
“They shall see the glory of Yahweh, the הֲדַר of our God”, beside the land’s own הֲדַר.

senses.gloss: majesty given (to the king, to man)
senses.definition: Splendour that Yahweh lays on the king he saves, and on man as he made him: not man’s own but given, as Yahweh’s challenge to Job shows.

evidence.note: Of the king: “his glory is great in your salvation; הוֹד וְהָדָר you lay upon him.”
Of man: “you made him a little lower than אֱלֹהִים, and crowned him with כָבוֹד וְהָדָר”, and gave him rule over the works of your hands (8:7). Heb 2:6–9 reads it of Jesus.
To the king: “gird your sword on your thigh, mighty one, your הוֹד and your הָדָר.”
“And in your הָדָר ride on prosperously, for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness.”
Yahweh to Job: “Deck yourself now with majesty and loftiness, and clothe yourself with הוֹד וְהָדָר”: a challenge Job cannot meet, for it is Yahweh’s to wear.
Of Joseph: “the firstborn of his bull, הָדָר is his, and his horns are the horns of a wild ox.”
The saints executing the judgement written on the nations and their kings: “this הָדָר is for all his חֲסִידִים.”

senses.gloss: splendour, adornment (of trees, land, city, people)
senses.definition: The beauty and fine appearance of a thing or a people: of trees and of a fruitful land, of a city or nation, of the strong and the old. It can be stripped away or go down to the grave, and the servant of Yahweh had none to look on.

evidence.note: At the feast of booths: “you shall take for yourselves on the first day פְּרִי עֵץ הָדָר, branches of palms, boughs of leafy trees and willows of the brook, and rejoice before Yahweh your God seven days.”
The desert blossoms: “the glory of Lebanon is given to it, the הֲדַר of Carmel and Sharon”: the splendour of forest and fruitful land.
To Jerusalem: “your beauty was perfect through my הָדָר which I had put upon you”: a splendour put on, as ornaments (16:11–13).
Of Tyre’s hired soldiers: “they hung shield and helmet in you; they gave you your הָדָר.”
“From the daughter of Zion all her הָדָר has gone”; her princes are like harts without pasture.
“The grave has enlarged its soul … and her הָדָר and her multitude and her pomp go down into it.”
“From their little children you take away my הָדָר for ever”: what Yahweh had given them.
“The glory (תִּפְאֶרֶת) of young men is their strength, and the הֲדַר of old men is the grey head.”
Of the woman of strength: “strength and הָדָר are her clothing.”
Of the servant: “he had no form (תֹאַר) nor הָדָר, that we should look on him, nor appearance, that we should desire him”: הָדָר is a splendour that is seen.

senses.definition: The plural in בְּהַדְרֵי־קֹדֶשׁ, the array in which the king’s people offer themselves on the day of his power, the same phrase as הַדְרַת־קֹדֶשׁ.

evidence.note: “Your people are freewill offerings in the day of your power, בְּהַדְרֵי־קֹדֶשׁ.”

Those who do not obey the gospel will be punished with everlasting destruction “from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his strength” (ἀπὸ τῆς δόξης τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ), the Septuagint’s words for Isa 2:10, 19, 21, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven (1:7).
Quoting Psa 8:6: “you crowned him with glory and honour (δόξῃ καὶ τιμῇ)”; τιμή stands for הָדָר, δόξα for כָבוֹד.
“We see Jesus, made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour.”

parallels.note: “Splendour, majesty”: הוֹד וְהָדָר is a fixed pair, of Yahweh and of the king.
“Glory”, beside it of man, of Yahweh and of his kingdom.
“Strength”, beside it as clothing and in the sanctuary.
“Beauty, glory”: the young man’s strength beside the old man’s grey head.
“Form, fine shape”, beside it of what the servant lacked.
“Majesty, loftiness”: Yahweh’s, with it in Isaiah’s refrain, and what Job is challenged to put on.

evidence.note: Taken on the first day of the feast of booths, beside palm branches, leafy boughs and willows. Scripture does not name the tree; in Neh 8:15 the people fetch olive, wild-olive, myrtle, palm and leafy branches to make the booths.

words.summary: To give הָדָר to someone: to honour a person, literally a face. In the law it is right toward the old and wrong in judgement, where it is favouring a party.

stems.gloss: honour; favour (in judgement); passive participle splendid

senses.definition: To show a person honour, rising before him and treating him as weighty: what is owed to the old.

evidence.note: “You shall rise up before the grey head and וְהָדַרְתָּ the face of the old man, and fear your God: I am Yahweh.” Rising is the outward act of it.

senses.definition: In a lawsuit, to give a party honour he has not earned by his cause, whether because he is great or because he is poor.

evidence.note: “You shall not lift up the face of the poor, nor תֶהְדַּר the face of the great; in righteousness you shall judge your neighbour.”
“Nor shall you תֶהְדַּר a poor man in his cause”: the same wrong toward the poor, set beside not following a crowd to pervert justice (23:2).

senses.definition: הָדוּר, adorned with splendour, of one in his clothing.

evidence.note: “Who is this that comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah, this one הָדוּר in his apparel, marching in the greatness of his strength?” Rev 19:13–15 takes up the figure of the garment and the winepress.

senses.definition: To be given the honour due: denied the elders of Judah by her conquerors.

evidence.note: “Princes are hanged by their hand; the faces of elders are not נֶהְדָּרוּ”: the reverse of Lev 19:32.

senses.definition: To give oneself honour: to take a great man’s place before the king.

evidence.note: “Do not תִּתְהַדַּר before the king, and do not stand in the place of the great; for better that he say to you, Come up here, than that you be put lower” (25:7). Jesus teaches the same at Luk 14:8–11.

greek.gloss: wonder at; (with πρόσωπον) admire a person, show partiality

evidence.note: Of the ungodly, “θαυμάζοντες πρόσωπα for the sake of advantage”: the Septuagint’s phrase for Lev 19:15.
“Honour all men … honour the king”: the word, though not a quotation of Lev 19:32.

parallels.note: “Lift the face”, favour: done to the poor as הָדַר is done to the great.

words.summary: Found only in construct: הַדְרַת־קֹדֶשׁ, the array of holiness in which Yahweh is worshipped, and הַדְרַת־מֶלֶךְ, a king’s splendour.

senses.definition: In הַדְרַת־קֹדֶשׁ, the splendour that belongs to holiness, in which Yahweh is to be worshipped and praised; whether the worshippers’ array or Yahweh’s holiness is meant, the text does not say, but trembling before him stands beside it.

evidence.note: “Give to Yahweh the glory of his name; bow down to Yahweh בְּהַדְרַת־קֹדֶשׁ.”
“Bow down to Yahweh בְּהַדְרַת־קֹדֶשׁ; tremble before him, all the earth.”
“Bring an offering and come before him; bow down to Yahweh בְּהַדְרַת־קֹדֶשׁ.”
Jehoshaphat sets singers to praise “לְהַדְרַת־קֹדֶשׁ” before the army, saying “Give thanks to Yahweh, for his חֶסֶד is for ever.”

senses.definition: A king’s splendour, which stands in the number of his people.

evidence.note: “In the multitude of people is the הַדְרַת־מֶלֶךְ, but in the want of people is the ruin of a prince.”

parallels.note: “Tremble before him”, beside worship in הַדְרַת־קֹדֶשׁ.

opposites.note: “Ruin” of a prince who lacks people, against a king’s הֲדָרָה.

words.summary: Once, of a kingdom’s splendour through which a tax-collector is sent; a by-form of הָדָר.

senses.definition: The glory of a kingdom, here the object of an exactor’s levy.

evidence.note: “Then shall stand up in his place one who makes an exactor pass through the הֶדֶר of the kingdom; but within a few days he shall be broken.”

senses.definition: To give honour to God, beside praising and exalting him; what Nebuchadnezzar did when humbled and Belshazzar did not.

evidence.note: “I blessed the Most High, and I praised and הַדְּרֵת him who lives for ever.”
“I praise and exalt and מְהַדַּר the King of heaven, for all his works are truth … and those who walk in pride he is able to humble.”
To Belshazzar: “the gods of silver and gold … you have praised, and the God in whose hand your breath is … you have not הַדַּרְתָּ.”

parallels.note: “Praise”, beside it each time in Daniel 4.

senses.definition: A king’s majesty, which Nebuchadnezzar boasted as his own but which the Most High gave, took away, and gave back.

evidence.note: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built … by the might of my power and for the glory of הַדְרִי?”
When his reason returned, “for the glory of my kingdom הַדְרִי and my brightness returned to me.”
“The Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father the kingdom and greatness and glory and הַדְרָה.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s New Testament has it once, in the phrase for Paul’s “to the praise of his glory”.

senses.definition: The glory of God that the redeemed are to show forth.

evidence.note: “That we should be לְהֶדְרָא of his praise, we who first hoped in Christ”, for Greek εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης αὐτοῦ.

words.summary: Once, of what Yahweh will make straight before Cyrus. The context fixes only that they are obstacles on a road; Jewish Aramaic הֲדוּרָא, “coil”, plural “winding road, steep ascent”, fits, but the link to the root’s sense of splendour is not clear. Its one token is counted under the verb’s key.

senses.gloss: rough, winding places on a road
senses.definition: Uneven ground that Yahweh levels before his anointed, set beside doors of bronze and bars of iron.

evidence.note: To Cyrus: “I will go before you and make the הֲדוּרִים straight; I will break in pieces doors of bronze and cut through bars of iron.” Compare Isa 40:4, the crooked made straight and the rough places a plain.

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic uses the pael for the Hebrew verb in the Targum of Lev 19:15, and the noun הֲדָרָא for Hebrew הָדָר and הֲדָרָה in the Targum of Proverbs (31:25; 14:28). The same Aramaic הֲדַר also means “go around, return”, which Jastrow treats as another sense of the letters.

evidence.note: “to honor, distinguish. Dan. IV, 31.—Targ. O. Lev. XIX, 15.”
“same [as הָדָר]. Targ. Prov. XXXI, 25 … Ib. XIV, 28.”
“adornment, crown, beauty, glory”; Pi. of הָדַר “to crown, adorn, distinguish”.

cognates.note: Jastrow compares the plural הְדוּרֵי, a field or road that can be climbed only by winding, with Isa 45:2. Goes with הֲדוּרִים only; whether it is the same root as “splendour” is not shown.

evidence.note: “coil, convolution … Pl. הְדוּרֵי (cmp. Is. XLV, 2) spiral road, a field which can be tilled only by spiral movements, steep hill. B. Bath. 12ᵃ.”

cognates.gloss: splendour (?); or a misreading of ḏrt “vision”
cognates.note: Wiktionary glosses Ugaritic hdrt “splendour” and compares הֲדָרָה. In Kirta’s dream (KTU 1.14), Segert reads the word as ḏrt “vision” (bḏrty, “in my vision”, beside bḥlmy “in my dream”), which is another root. Not counted until a reading is settled.

evidence.note: “splendour”; “Compare Hebrew הֲדָרָה.”

evidence.locator: glossary, s.v. ḏrt; selected texts, Keret’s dream-vision (1.14 III)
evidence.note: ḏrt “vision”; “bdrty.ab.adm” beside “bhlmy.il.ytn”.

doctrine.statement: Yahweh is “clothed with הוֹד וְהָדָר” (Psa 104:1); they are “before him” in his sanctuary (Psa 96:6; 1Ch 16:27), and his work is such (Psa 111:3). Isaiah says that in the day Yahweh rises to shake the earth men will go into the rocks “from the terror of Yahweh and from the splendour of his majesty”, and the lofty will be brought low and Yahweh alone exalted (Isa 2:10–21). Paul takes up those words for the day “the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels”, when those who do not obey the gospel are punished with everlasting destruction “from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his strength” (2Th 1:7–9). From the verses: the majesty is Yahweh’s, worn as a king’s robe, and it is shown in the Son at his coming, to the ruin of all that is proud.

Yahweh challenges Job to “clothe yourself with הוֹד וְהָדָר” and save himself by his own hand (Job 40:10–14), which he cannot. Nebuchadnezzar boasted of Babylon built “for the glory of my majesty” (Dan 4:27), was driven out until he knew “that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men” (4:29), and when his majesty returned he glorified the King of heaven, who “is able to humble those who walk in pride” (4:33–34); Daniel tells Belshazzar that the Most High had given his father that majesty, and that he himself had not glorified the God in whose hand his breath was (Dan 5:18–23). The king of Israel has הוֹד וְהָדָר because Yahweh lays them on him in his salvation (Psa 21:6), and the old man’s grey head is his הָדָר (Pro 20:29). From the verses: splendour in man is a gift, held under God, and taken away when it is claimed as one’s own.

Isaiah’s servant grew up “as a root out of dry ground”, with “no form nor הָדָר that we should look on him” (Isa 53:2), was despised, and poured out his soul to death (53:3, 12). Psalm 8 says that God made man a little lower than אֱלֹהִים and crowned him with כָבוֹד וְהָדָר, putting all things under his feet (Psa 8:6–7); Hebrews reads it of Jesus, “made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour” (Heb 2:6–9). Psalm 45 bids the king gird on his הוֹד and הָדָר and ride out for truth and righteousness (Psa 45:4–5), and Hebrews applies that psalm to the Son (Heb 1:8–9). Psalm 149 ends, of the saints who execute judgement on the nations, “this הָדָר is for all his חֲסִידִים” (Psa 149:9), and Paul says “the saints shall judge the world” (1Co 6:2). From the verses: Jesus had no splendour of his own in his life, but was crowned by God after his death, and the same honour is promised to those who are his.

The law commands Israel to rise before the grey head and “honour (הָדַר) the face of the old man” (Lev 19:32), and in the same chapter forbids honouring “the face of the great” in judgement, as it forbids lifting up the face of the poor (Lev 19:15; Exo 23:3). James, citing the royal law of Lev 19:18, says that to give the rich man the good seat and the poor man the floor is to “have respect of persons” and so to sin (Jas 2:1–9); Jude marks the ungodly as those who admire persons for advantage (Jud 1:16). From the verses: honour is owed where God sets it, to age and to himself (Lev 19:32), but in judgement neither wealth nor poverty may weigh against righteousness.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13 for Leviticus 23 (פְּרִי עֵץ הָדָר, Lev 23:40). Verse numbers are the Hebrew text’s (Psa 8:6 = English 8:5; Psa 21:6 = 21:5; Psa 45:4–5 = 45:3–4; Dan 4:27–34 = English 4:30–37). Names left out: הֲדַר, the Edomite king of Gen 36:39 (e.as.ae; written הֲדַד at 1Ch 1:50), and הֲדֹרָם, Hadoram (e.as.af, also filed under e.ao.ae), whose link to this root is unshown; neither key is claimed here. BDB key e.as.ac also counts Gen 36:39 (the name), so its use count is one high; e.as.ae in turn lists Isa 35:2 (twice) and Psa 145:5, 12, which are the noun. Isa 45:2 הֲדוּרִים is kept as its own word with no key, since its one token is filed under the verb (e.as.aa, no stem); the Qumran Isaiah scroll and the Septuagint (ὄρη) read הררים “mountains”, which is not followed here. The tree of Lev 23:40 is not named by scripture; the identification with the citron is tradition and is not entered. Arabic هدر (Lane pp. 2885–2886: blood “went for nothing”; a camel “brayed”; wine “fermented”; thunder “rumbled”) shares the letters but not the meaning and is not entered; nor is Akkadian adāru “fear” (Oracc), which lacks the h. Segert’s Ugaritic glossary has no hdr “splendour”; the Wiktionary hdrt is entered as possible only. The Peshitta’s ܗܕܪܐ (SEDRA lexeme 779, root 491: “ornament, splendor, embellishment, honour”) occurs once, Eph 1:12; Payne Smith not consulted. Not consulted: Phoenician (nothing under H-D-R in Krahmalkov’s text layer), Geʿez, DULAT. Open questions for review: (1) Dan 11:20, the exactor through the הֶדֶר of the kingdom, is glossed without naming the king; (2) הַדְרַת־קֹדֶשׁ left open between the worshippers’ array and Yahweh’s holiness; (3) Rev 19:13 cited as taking up Isa 63:1; (4) 1Pe 2:17 under τιμάω is the word only, not a quotation.
